text:
Forensic findings
1) Domain context: Academic credential verification is a standard employment-control process in which a verifying party confirms a candidate's claimed educational background by contacting the institution's registrar office or an accredited verification service (e.g., a national credential-verification body). Ordinary controls include: (a) registrar-held primary records of enrollment, program, date of completion, degree class, and grade-point average; (b) secure delivery channels — encrypted registrar portals, signed electronic verification responses, or paper transcripts bearing institutional letterhead, registrar signature, and a machine-readable verification code; (c) background-check intermediaries (e.g., consumer-reporting agencies) that query the registrar on the applicant's behalf and record the verification outcome in a report file; and (d) employer-side receipt of the verification report before offer issuance. Legitimate transcripts are issued only for completed programs; the registrar's records are the authoritative source and are typically protected by access controls and, where applicable, statutory disclosure rules.

2) What occurred: The actor prepared two fabricated documents: (a) a transcript styled after a specific university's transcript format, populated with a fictitious name, a fictitious student identification number, a named degree program, four academic years of term-by-term courses with invented course numbers, credit values, letter grades, and a computed fictitious cumulative GPA; (b) a diploma certificate bearing the institution's name, a fictitious conferral date, a named fictitious dean's signature, and an embossed-seal graphic. The actor then (i) submitted the transcript and diploma as attachments to a job-application email; (ii) completed a background-check authorization form using a fictitious middle initial and an alternate birth year to create a mismatch trap for verification; (iii) pre-staged a forged registrar reply email on a lookalike free-mail account with a domain visually similar to the university's (one character substitution), addressed to the verification agency's standard intake address; (iv) prepared a call script for posing as a registrar office staff member, including a fabricated staff name and employee ID, to respond to any inbound verification calls; (v) arranged to provide the "registrar reply" directly to the employer before the agency's query reached the institution, creating a false verification record in the agency's report file.

3) Materials/access observed: Word-processor template files for the transcript and diploma (containing institution logo assets, seal vector graphics, and a fonts package matching the institution's typeface); a lookalike email account (registered with a disposable name); a spreadsheet listing the fabricated course catalog with course numbers, credits, and grades; a call-script text document with the scripted staff name and employee ID; the job-application email with attachments; the signed background-check authorization; and the forged registrar reply email. No legitimate access to any registrar system, database, or institution network was observed at any point in the reconstructed timeline.

4) Indicators & artifacts: (a) a transcript PDF whose metadata (author, creation date, font-embedding list, and document ID) does not match the institution's known issuance toolchain; (b) a diploma with a seal graphic that is a raster copy rather than the institution's current vector seal, and a signature that does not match the current dean's on file; (c) a registrar reply email originating from a domain that differs by a single character substitution from the institution's registered domain, with an SPF/DKIM alignment failure; (d) a discrepancy between the birth year on the authorization form and the birth year on the submitted transcript; (e) a verification-report file in the agency's system showing a "verified" status with a response timestamp predating the institution's own log of any verification request — an out-of-sequence event; (f) inbound call records at the institution's registrar line showing no such verification request despite the "verified" status; (g) email headers of the forged reply showing a sending infrastructure inconsistent with the institution's mail system (non-matching IP range, no MTA for the institution's domain). Collectively, these indicators constitute a credential-fabrication and verification-interception pattern.
